column1: # How well each table's digits are known.
# One line per table: tid, level, and the evidence for it. Read by
# `manage.py set_rigour`, which writes the level into the table's Data
# properties. Kept as a file rather than done in a script so that the
# judgement can be read, argued with and corrected -- it is a claim about
# 88 tables and most of it was made by reading one line of each generator.
# The evidence is the generate.sage that produced the table, in the
# numberdb-data repository, or -- for the fifteen tables that have no script --
# what was done to establish the digits here, recorded in the fourth column.
# An optional fourth column gives a table its own `rigour details` sentence,
# replacing the generic one for its level. It is there because `proven` covers
# more than one kind of thing: usually ball arithmetic, but T5's interval is a
# pair of theorems about matrix multiplication and T3's zeros were checked
# against arb's certified enclosures. A sentence that is nearly right is worse
# than none, since it is the sentence a reader will believe.
# The four physical constants are `measured`, which is not on the scale the
# other levels sit on. It says the number was not computed at all, so asking
# whether measurement beats agreement-checking has no answer -- they are not
# A first pass classified these by pattern-matching the scripts and got
# thirteen wrong, in three separate ways: `mpmath.mp.airyaizero(` does not
# match `mpmath\.\w+\(`; `from mpmath import mp` hides mpmath behind `mp`;
# and six p-adic scripts import mpmath, never call it, and compute in Qp,
# which tracks precision exactly as an interval field does. Every line that
# is not `exact` by the table's declared type has since been read.
# The direction that matters was checked separately: a wrong `heuristic` is
# conservative, a wrong `proven` is a false claim of rigour. Every `proven`
# was re-checked against a deliberately wide net for inexact arithmetic, and
# the one hit turned out to be a `.n()` inside a debugging print.
# That check was not enough. Reading a script cannot tell you whether
# `RIF(f(x))` is an enclosure: it depends on whether f has an interval
# implementation, and when it does not, Sage evaluates numerically and hands
# back an interval of width zero -- which looks exactly like an exact value.
# Running each function settled it. gamma, psi, zeta and log return genuine
# enclosures; elliptic_kc, elliptic_ec, elliptic_pi and sin_integral return
# points that do not contain a 4000-bit value. Four tables were labelled
# `proven` on that basis and are now `heuristic`. Their stored digits are
# right -- they agree with a 4000-bit computation past 200 characters -- but
# nothing proves them, which is the distinction this file exists to draw.
# A table with a generator in `generators/` is described by that generator,
# not by this file: the generator is what runs, and it may do better than the
# script it replaced. Nine lines below say `converted:` for that reason, and
# running this file with --overwrite before they did cost those nine tables
# their levels for about a minute.

column4: Rests on mpmath's stieltjes, which evaluates a contour integral by numerical quadrature. mpmath's quadrature returns an error *estimate*, and its own documentation says the result may still be inaccurate for some functions; the working precision it uses is the requested precision plus ten bits and the square root of n, which for the largest n here is about forty. The interval was then widened by four units in the last place, a bound asserted rather than derived. Recomputing at double precision agrees to about 104 digits, so the hundred written are very likely right.

PARI ellheight documents no accuracy; see the details
column4: Computed with Sage's E.regulator(proof=True). The arithmetic is proven: proof=True means the Mordell-Weil basis is certified, so the regulator is the right quantity rather than a multiple of it. The numerics are not. The heights come from PARI's ellheight, whose documentation states the normalisation and nothing about accuracy; Sage's own implementation truncates Silverman's series at a term count derived from his published bound, but tracks no rounding error through the loop, and its working precision is a guard found by patching cases that failed. The height pairing matrix is then built in ordinary floating point, its off-diagonal entries by a subtraction of nearly equal heights, and a determinant is taken. Recomputing at double precision agrees to about 204 digits, so the hundred written here are almost certainly right; nothing bounds them.

the script computes at two precisions and asserts they agree
column4: Computed at two working precisions, the second twice the first, and written only after the two agreed -- the script asserts it. That bounds the error from working precision and nothing else: L-values are computed by a truncated approximate functional equation, and two runs of the same method agree even where the method is wrong. The interval was also widened by four units in the last place, but at a precision far finer than the digits written, so that widening is not what the digits rest on.
